title: Why Stars Twinkle
dir: Listen while your teacher reads about stars. Then answer each question out loud.
text: Why Stars Twinkle A star does not blink. Far out in space it shines with a steady light. The twinkle happens much closer to you, in the air above your head. Air is always moving. Warm air bends light a little more than cold air does. The moving air slides past. The thin beam of starlight bends this way and that. From the ground the star seems to jump and flicker. A planet looks steadier. A planet is close enough to show a tiny disk. It shows a disk instead of a single point. Astronauts above the air see stars that do not twinkle at all.
qs: What makes a star seem to twinkle?
Where does the twinkle happen?
Why does a planet look steadier than a star?

title: What a Seed Needs
dir: Listen while your teacher reads the facts. Then listen to each question and answer out loud.
text: What a Seed Needs A seed is a tiny plant. It has its own lunch. The lunch is packed around it. The seed stays dry and still. It waits until three things reach it. First it needs water. The coat around it is hard. Water makes it soften. Next it needs air. That is why good soil is never packed down too tight. Last it needs warmth. When all three arrive, the coat splits. A small white root pushes down.

title: Why It Rains
dir: Listen while your teacher reads about rain. Then answer each question out loud.
text: Why It Rains Every day the sun warms the top of the ocean. Some of that water turns into a gas you cannot see. The gas rises with the warm air. High up, the air is cold, and the cold turns the gas back into tiny drops. Millions of those drops floating together are what you see as a cloud. The drops bump into each other and join up. A drop gets too heavy for the air to hold. Then it falls. That is rain. The same water has been going around like this for a very long time.
qs: What does the sun do to the top of the ocean?

text: The Two Rows Ravi was given a packet of bean seeds. He planted them in two short rows. He watered both rows the same. But he could not stop wondering about the row by the fence. title: How a Band Stays Together
dir: Listen while your teacher reads about marching bands. Then answer each question out loud.
text: How a Band Stays Together A marching band has nobody out in front waving a stick. The players are all moving. Most of them cannot see each other. So a band holds together by sound instead. The bass drum lays down a steady beat. The beat is low and loud. Every player steps on it. Sound travels about a thousand feet in one second. That seems quick. But a long band can stretch far enough. The players at the back hear the drum a little late. Good bands fix this by watching the feet ahead of them as well as listening.
qs: What does a marching band use instead of somebody waving a stick out front?
Why can the players not simply watch one another?

title: The Squirrel and the Ribbon

text: The Squirrel and the Ribbon A squirrel found a long red ribbon lying on the grass after the school show. This is the finest thing in the whole wood, she said. title: Two Who Made a Difference
dir: Listen while your teacher reads about him. Answer out loud.
text: George Washington Carver was born into slavery. It was in Missouri. He was set free as a small child. He wanted to learn so badly. He walked miles to a school. That school would take him. Later he worked his way through college. He became a scientist who studied plants. Farmers near him grew cotton. They grew it year after year. Their soil wore out. Their crops failed. Carver showed them something. They could plant peanuts and sweet potatoes. That put the goodness back in the soil. Then he found hundreds of uses for those crops. So farmers could sell them. He gave his findings away free. He taught poor farmers on a wagon. He drove it from farm to farm.
